Thank you very much Finn!

On Tuesday, 26 September 2023 at 15:41:52 UTC+2 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Hi, I'm not entirely sure what the question is, as the "predictive
> posterior estimates" on the data level _is_ what you get by using
> inla.posterior.sample to sample the latent variables and then from
> that sample the data level.
>
> But if you mean how to compare the posterior predictive samples to the
> observed sample distribution, then there are several ways, depending
> on the specific aspect being investigated (e.g. spatial prediction
> would be treated differently to the "overall marginal distribution",
> etc).
> Might help if you have a more specific question in mind regarding what
> aspect of the predictions you want to investigate; leave-site-out
> prediction being one possible choice.
>
> I believe there's one or more papers by Aki Vehtari and colleagues
> about how to assess posterior predictive samples. (e.g. with
> probability integral transform histograms and/or
> Kolmogorov-Smirnov-type CDF difference comparisons, etc)
>
> Finn
>
> On Tue, 26 Sept 2023 at 13:59, TheCorinna1994 <corinn...@hotmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Finn,
> >
> > I have one final question though: when i draw monte carlo samples with inla.posterior.sample from the bgev distribution and compute the predictor at my unobserved locations and compare them to what I get from including the prediction scenario in the INLA fitting process, how can I relate this to the predictive posterior estimates? Do these histogram give me a good measure on how well my fitting process went?
> >
> > Sorry for this stupid question but highly appreciate your answer.
> >
> > Thanks so far for your great anwers.
> >
> > All the best,
> > Corinna
> >
> > On Tuesday, 19 September 2023 at 15:39:29 UTC+2 Finn Lindgren wrote:
> >>
> >> Hi Corinna,
> >>
> >> the observed value will usually have more variability than the posterior mean of the location parameter for the observation model.
> >>
> >> For example:
> >> Take a simpler case, with a predictor \eta_i observed with additive Gaussian noise, to get y_i = \eta_i + \epsilon_i, where \epsilon_i ~ N(0, \sigma^2)
> >> Then even if we could perfectly estimate \eta_i, then the spread of values would be smaller than for y_i, because of the contribution from the \epsilon_i.
> >>
> >> This is also the case for the bgev distribution model, and virtually _every_ observation model; furthermore, generally in spatial statistics when there's a Gaussian field involved in the model for \eta, the posterior mean for \eta will be fundamentally smoother across space than the observations, and have smaller variability.
> >>
> >> The quetion I think you need to consider is instead whether the posterior predictive distribution for y_i resembles the observed values.
> >> In the Gaussian case, one can simply add&subtract a quantile of the \epsilon-distribution, but for bgev I assume it would involve either posterior sampling on the data level, or some quantile calculations. Posterior predictive sampling is the most general approach, as it allows any type of model.
> >>
> >> Finn
> >>

messages.subject_clean: Joint model: compund symmtery and correlated random effects
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community

I want to fit a joint Binomial-Poisson areal model with this definition :

r_ij  ~ Binomial (n_ij, p_ij )
logit⁡(p_ij)= β_0,1 + β_1,1[agecat_1]_ij + β_2,1[agecat_2]_ij + ν_(i,1) + γ_(j,1)

O_ij  ~ Poisson (N_ij,IR_ij )
log⁡(IR_ij)= β_0,2+β_1,2 [agecat_1]_ij + β_2,2[agecat_2]_ij + ν_(i,2) + γ_(j,2)

with ν_(i,1) & ν_(i,2) spatial structured random effect, γ_(j,1) & γ_(j,2) temporal structured random effect, i = areal unit (1,...,93), and j = temporal unit (1,...,16).

I plan to compare different structures of the variance-covariance matrix of the random effects, in particular, the compound symmetry model and correlated random effects. If I understand correctly I can model the compound symmetry using the 'group' option:

mod.compund <- Y ~ -1 + intercept +
  cov.bin + cov.pois +
  f(idarea2, model = "besag", graph = gDIST, group = g.nu <http://g.nu>) +
  f(idperiod2, model = "rw1", group = g.gamma)

My question will be, how I can fit the correlated random effects with the below matrix? Is it still using the 'group' option?

Thank you.

Kind regards,
Yessika

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] SEM model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

> Is there an explanation for the slm effect of the model in this picture? For example, do darker areas have more influence on the dependent variable? How to explain the influence of spatial aggregation effect on dependent variables in SEM model?  Thank you.

This is not really an INLA question but I will try to answer it. Those estimates (posterior means?) are part of the linear predictor, hence, they will be influencing the mean (assuming a normal model). So you can expect larger values of the response where you observe darker areas (ceteris paribus). I am not sure what you mean by “the influence of spatial aggregation”. If you mean a change of support (i.e., considering larger areas) then  you will most likely find some differences as you are observing a (spatial) process at a different scale. If you mean interaction between areas, then you need to compute the impacts [1].

Best,

Virgilio

[1] https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7390/9/17/2044

to inla(...)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Seth,

Simply add control.predictor=list(link= 1). The number refers to the number of the response. So always 1, unless you are using multiple response variables in the same model.

fit <- bru(y ~ age,  family = "binomial", data = df, control.predictor=list(link= 1))

Hi All,

I am hoping you can help me with my error. I am running a mixed conditional Poisson regression but am quite new to INLA so do not understand the output of the errors. I have attached the error outputs. For some data, this runs fine and for others, I get the attached errors and I do not understand why. Any help would be much appreciated.

The first attachment (error_INLA_01.txt) is when I ran the model with verbose=TRUE and the second (error_INLA_02.txt) is when I ran it with verbose=TRUE,debug=TRUE, safe=FALSE.

Inla formula:
formula.ndvi <- case ~  -1 +
  ndvi_norm +
  ndvi_norm:log_sl +
  ndvi_norm:cos_ta +
  f(strt_n, model="iid", hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1e-6),
                                                   fixed = TRUE))) +
  f(ID_ndvi, ndvi_norm, values = 1:length(unique(dat$ind_f)), model="iid",
    hyper = list(theta = list(initial = log(1), fixed = FALSE,
                              prior = "pc.prec",param = c(1, 0.05))))

I ran the model:
inla.ndvi <- inla(formula.ndvi, family = "Poisson", data = dat,
                     control.fixed = list(
                       mean = mean.beta,
                       prec = list(default = prec.beta)),
                     control.compute = list(
                       dic = TRUE,
                       return.marginals.predictor=TRUE),
                     verbose=TRUE,debug=TRUE,safe=FALSE,
                     num.threads='2:1')

I have had different errors that I think may be a separate issues e.g.:
errors:
*** max_correction = 25.01 >= 25.00, so 'vb.correction' is aborted
*** Please (re-)consider your model, priors, confounding, etc.
*** You can change the emergency value (current value=25.00) by
***  'control.inla=list(control.vb=list(emergency=...))'

I appreciate any help and advice.

Thank you,

Leila

Hi,

this sounds like the kind of problem
https://github.com/finnlindgren/multiprobit was made for; I started
developing it for some early Covid response modelling but the project
ended up not going ahead. The package seemed to do the job though, by
doing a numerically efficient multivariate probit model estimation.

(There may also be a way to approach this with inla itself, which
isn't used by multiprobit, but the number of correlation parameters
may be a bit much for inla. multiprobit instead uses a latent Gaussian
parameterisation of the correlation matrix, and uses the "excursions"
package for numerical fast multivariate Gaussian probability
calculations.)

Finn

messages.body_plain:
There is this model 'iidkd'  which can do multivariate random effects in
dimension=k. the parameterisation is better than iid4d f.ex. there is
also work underway (on arxiv in a month?) about a new take on how to
model structured correlation matrices with causual interpretation, so we
can go higher in dimension k but avoid that the number of parameters
grows like O(k^2).

in short, you can do dependence between the latent model, but less
within the observations (directly), except multinomial (see vignette),
composite data (see  https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.13928 ), and of'course,
normal data.

Best
H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Competing risks joint models using R-INLA
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Competing risks joint models using R-INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the _inputs_ to the model components define for what covariate or
index value the effect should be calculated.
The _output_ contains the numerical values of those effects.

It's not clear what problem it is you're trying to solve. If you want
to evaluate the posterior expectation of an spde effect at given
locations, use for example
  fm_evaluate(mesh, loc = locations_for_evaluation, field =
result$summary.random$your_field_component$mean)
(inla.mesh.project() in old INLA versions, which now calls
fmesher::fm_evaluate() internally).
You can also get the mapping matrix from mesh node values (as stored
in summary.random) to locations with
  A <- fm_basis(mesh, loc = locations_for_evaluation)
(or inla.spde.make.A() in old INLA versions, which now calls
fmesher::fm_basis() internally)

For more complex evaluations (e.g. quantiles etc), combine it with
inla.posterior.sample().

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear R-INLA group,

Thank you very much for your response. When referencing the code in the paper "Competing risks joint models using R-INLA," I had a concern. If the BYM2 model is used for the space, then the "idareaL" of "random.eff" can be used directly. However, if the SPDE model is used for the space, the "s" in "indexes <- inla.spde.make.index("s", n.spde = spde$n.spde)" can be included in "random.eff." Nevertheless, when using the inla() function, it shows that "s" cannot be found (Perhaps because s is a data group and idareaL is a column of numbers?). How should I adjust it if I want to use the SPDE model?

fixed.eff<-data.frame(mu=as.factor(c(rep(1,nL),rep(2,nS),rep(3,nS))),

                      ageL=c(dataL$Age,rep(0,nS),rep(0,nS)),

                      age1=c(rep(0,nL),dataS$Age,rep(0,nS)),

                      age2=c(rep(0,nL),rep(0,nS),dataS$Age))

random.eff<-list(timeL=c(dataL$Time,rep(NA,nS),rep(NA,nS)),

                 idareaL=c(dataL$idarea,rep(NA,nS),rep(NA,nS)),

                 Lr1 = c(dataL$code, rep(NA, nS), rep(NA, nS)),

                 Lr2 = c(dataL$code, rep(NA, nS), rep(NA, nS)),

                 C1r1 = c(rep(NA, nL), dataS$code, rep(NA, nS)),

                 C1r2 = c(rep(NA, nL), dataS$code, rep(NA, nS)),

                 C2r1 = c(rep(NA, nL), rep(NA, nS), dataS$code),

                 C2r2 = c(rep(NA, nL), rep(NA, nS), dataS$code)))

jointdata<-c(fixed.eff,random.eff)

y.long <- c(dataL$logCD4,rep(NA, nS),rep(NA,nS))

y.survC1 <- inla.surv(time = c(rep(NA, nL),dataS$Time,rep(NA,nS)), event = c(rep(NA, nL),dataE1$event,rep(NA,nS)))

y.survC2 <- inla.surv(time = c(rep(NA, nL), rep(NA,nS),dataS$Time), event = c(rep(NA, nL),rep(NA,nS),dataE2$event))

y.joint<-list(y.long,y.survC1,y.survC2)

jointdata$Y=y.joint

formula.model=Y~-1+mu+age1+age2+

f(inla.group(timeL,n=50),model="rw2",scale.model = TRUE,

    hyper = list(prec = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01))))+

  f(idareaL, model = "bym2", graph = g, hyper = list

  (prec = list(prior = "pc.prec",param = c(0.5 / 0.31, 0.01)),

  phi = list(prior = "pc",param = c(0.5, 2 / 3))))+

  f(Lr1, model="iid")+

  f(C1r1, copy="Lr1")+

  f(C2r1, copy="Lr1")

Jointmodel= inla(formula.model, family = c("gaussian","weibullsurv","weibullsurv"),

                 data = jointdata, verbose=TRUE)

summary(Jointmodel)

Thanks,

Masuma

> Hi,
>
> the _inputs_ to the model components define for what covariate or
> index value the effect should be calculated.
> The _output_ contains the numerical values of those effects.
>
> It's not clear what problem it is you're trying to solve. If you want
> to evaluate the posterior expectation of an spde effect at given
> locations, use for example
> fm_evaluate(mesh, loc = locations_for_evaluation, field =
> result$summary.random$your_field_component$mean)
> (inla.mesh.project() in old INLA versions, which now calls
> fmesher::fm_evaluate() internally).
> You can also get the mapping matrix from mesh node values (as stored
> in summary.random) to locations with
> A <- fm_basis(mesh, loc = locations_for_evaluation)
> (or inla.spde.make.A() in old INLA versions, which now calls
> fmesher::fm_basis() internally)
>
> For more complex evaluations (e.g. quantiles etc), combine it with
> inla.posterior.sample().
>
> Finn
>

messages.subject_clean: ngvb package
messages.body_plain:
Hello, I am having some difficulty using the proposed ngvb package.

It seems to work fine with a simple "iid" random effect.  However, with an "ar1" replicate, it no longer works, although "ar1" is said to be a supported structure as long as the "pc.cor0" prior is used.

consider this INLA model, which works fine:

-----------

library(INLA)
library(ngvb)

pc.ar1 <- list(theta1 = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(.5, 0.01)),
               theta2 = list(prior="pc.cor0", param=c(.5, 0.01)) )

set.seed(1234)
inla.1 <- inla(bip ~ f(xx1, replicate = xx2, model="ar1",
                       hyper = pc.ar1),
               data = df %>%
                 dplyr::mutate(xx1 = as.integer(factor(x1)),
                               xx2 = as.integer(factor(x2))),
               Ntrials = pa,
               family = "binomial",
               verbose = TRUE, debug = TRUE
               num.threads = 1,
               control.inla = list(int.strategy = 'eb'),
               control.compute = list(config = TRUE, waic = TRUE, mlik = TRUE)
               )

-----------

But then the ng.check command has some sort of indexing problem and the ngvb command crashes outright. The issue seems to be around the formation of the predictor, but it is not clear to me if that is actually the problem or this could just be a sign of not enough memory.

messages.subject: Gradients calculations in R-INLA?
messages.subject_clean: Gradients calculations in R-INLA?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Would you be able to tell me about how first and second derivatives are obtained in R-INLA? That is:

1) The first derivatives used to perform gradient-based optimisation to find modes.
2) The second derivatives used to calculate Hessian matrices.

Based on the logs, I know that central finite differences are used. Is this for both the first and second derivatives? Is there a way in which the set of models specified in R-INLA are utilised to (efficiently) precalculate any aspect of the derivatives? Were there particular design criteria you had for the R-INLA software as to why numerical methods were preferred to automatic differentiation (like TMB <https://kaskr.github.io/adcomp/Introduction.html> say)?

Apologies if I'm missing something in the documentation about these details!

Best wishes,
Adam <https://athowes.github.io/>

Hi,

the gradients and hessian are computed like described here

https://www.aimsciences.org/article/doi/10.3934/fods.2021037

using finite differences. this 'smart gradients' really just work.

finite differences parallelise nicely as discussed here

https://www.aimsciences.org/article/doi/10.3934/fods.2021037

and the number of hyperparmeters are moderate so it is ok, and allow us
to have good parallel performance.

we're also using, extensively, external sparse matrix libraries, which
needs to be adapted to AD if that is the goal, which you can read about
on STAN blogs how straight forward that is.

hope this helps.
H

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

We are trying to use `inlabru` to estimate the population size of a group-living
speciesin a protected area, but we would really appreciate some input, as we are quite new to inlabru etc.

We have counted animals in groups from observations points / plots, with 6
surveys at (most of) each plot, although we pool these surveys together for the
time being. We only observed ~ 110 groups are each survey (513 groups total)
  over a fairly large area, so we'll probably have to stick to simple models.

In addition to modeling the location of groups in space through the SPDE, we
model group size as exponentially distributed, but otherwise 'constant' in space
(ie group size does not depend on the location in space).

Would someone be so kind as to have a look at our script (attached) and let us
know whether we're doing something blatantly wrong ?

In particular, our results have been varying enormously with the mesh and priors
for the Matern correlation structure, as well as with building the integration
points for obtaining the predictions.

We understand such variation based on the mesh etc. is to be expected to some
extent... However, we would really appreciate if someone had recommendations and tips to ensure we have all this set up "correctly" before we move on with this analysis.

Thank you in advance for you valuable help!

Olivier

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
your INLA version is too old compared with your Matrix package
version. Best would be to upgrade INLA.

However, the current INLA version says that inla.mesh.create.helper()
was deprecated "a very long time ago".
Even _its_ replacement function, inla.mesh.2d() is now deprecated (but
will stick around for quite a while most likely), in favour of
fmesher::fm_mesh_2d_inla()
that has the same syntax as inla.mesh.2d(). Just rename the points and
points.domain arguments to loc and loc.domain.
Install the fmesher package to access it, and then you should be able
to build the mesh even with your old INLA version.
But presumably you want to use the mesh in an inla() model, and then
you may still need to upgrade INLA.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] General recommendations / integration points
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] General recommendations / integration points
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

it's not entirely clear from the code what kind of observation model
you're intending to use, but presumably you are using the actual
_locations_ of points within each plot, so it's a point process model
over the "space-times-size" product domain?
That's at least what the code is setup to do, and I don't see anything
immediately wrong with the structure.

A general observation: Setting a more specific prior distribution on
log.r would likely help, as I expect it to be strongly confounded with
the Intercept.  See the development version of inlabru that has a new
feature for converting components into non-Gaussians (via
marginal=bru_mapper_marginal(...)).
With the CRAN version, at least do log.r(1, prec.linear = 1) or
similar, to discourage extreme values.

The predict() step should be insensitive to the integration scheme,
but the modelling step might be more sensitive.
Might be sensible to plot the integration scheme to see what it's doing?

Use
ips <- fm_int(domain = list(size=size_domain,
geometry=geometry_domain), samplers = plots22_sf)
ggplot() + gg(geometry_domain) + geom_sf(data=ips %>% filter(size ==
size_domain$loc[1]), aes(size = weight))

The one part I'm uncertain about is your predict() fm_int construction, with
    samplers = list(
      size = NULL,
      geometry = plots22_sf # 101 survey points
    )

Do you get the same integration points if you set
    samplers = list(
      geometry = plots22_sf # 101 survey points
    )
?
Specifically, what happens with "size" in the fm_int() output?
You do need size to be _something_ in the integration points; unclear
if you want to predict for a specific size, or integrate over all of
them.

Finn

Is there a reason you have this intuition? When you write "in a multicore environment" that's because AD ultimately wouldn't perform as well in a parallel setting as other methods?

When you write "AD for the hyperparameters" I assume this refers to the gradient of the Laplace approximation. Do you have any thoughts about AD to calculate the Laplace approximation itself (as in, not AD for the hyperparameters, but AD for the latent field to arrive at its Gaussian approximation)? Is there a way in which calculation of these latent field precision matrices is sped up by knowledge of the structure (something like this is what I was aiming to get at when asking "Is there a way in which the set of models specified in R-INLA are utilised to (efficiently) precalculate any aspect of the derivatives?")?

And yes, I am sure anyone would have difficulty implementing the INLA algorithm more efficiently than R-INLA! A huge amount of work has gone into this software (some of it quite technical and difficult to grasp from the outside!) so thanks to yourself and the other developers for doing this. Part of the motivation I have for investigating AD is that the models the scientists I work with use are often not compatible with R-INLA, as much as they might like to use it.

Adam

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Gradients calculations in R-INLA?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Gradients calculations in R-INLA?
messages.body_plain:
I can answer this from the inlabru perspective;

in "plain" INLA, all the likelihoods and their derivatives with
respect to the linear predictor are hand-coded (I believe). Since each
observation is linked to the latent field via a single element of the
linear predictor, the chain rule is explicit; just the individual
likelihood derivatives, combined with the fixed model matrix for the
linear predictor. For that AD wouldn't really add anything except the
possibility of simplifying some kind of user-defined likelihood
capability.

For inlabru however, we _would_ benefit from AD for models with
non-linear predictors, as it currently uses numerical derivatives to
evaluate the Jacobian and construct the sequence of linearised
predictor models that is passed on to INLA.
Currently, this linearisation step is slow for some models in ways
that AD might help with.  The "bru_mapper" system used to construct
the link between latent variables, effects, and the predictor
expression, is setup to facilitate some simple AD behaviour, but if it
could "hook" into an existing AD system for R expressions, that could
speed things up (though inlabru 2.9.0 saw some significant speedups
just from dealing with the most obvious bottlenecks indicated by the R
profiler).

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Yesterday, I raised a concern about mesh creation, and you suggested using "fmesher::fm_mesh_2d_inla()." I've now utilized this function to generate a mesh, which I intend to employ in a spatio-temporal analysis with the INLA model. However, I've observed that the process of mesh creation is exceedingly time-consuming. In fact, I initiated it yesterday and allowed it to run overnight, but it's still ongoing. I'm wondering whether the arguments I've used in the "fm_mesh_2d_inla()" function, such as "max.edge" and "min.angle," are affecting the time it takes to create the mesh, or if the extended duration is due to limitations in my computer hardware.

These are some of the codes i am using

library (INLA)
library (fields)
library(readr)
library(sp)
library(fmesher)
memory.limit ()
memory . limit ( size =211631800000)
setwd("D:/ DATASETs")
borders <- read.csv("amhara region border.csv ")
head(borders)
index <- dim(borders)[1]
plot(borders)
BB1=borders[borders$X<320000 & borders$X>300000 & borders$Y<1350000 & borders$Y>1250000,]
BB=borders[-c(2875:2906),]
plot(BB,type="l",lwd=3)
coordinates <- read.csv("coordinates.csv")
head(coordinates)
coordinates_val <- read.csv("coordinates_Val.csv")
head(coordinates_val )
data <- read.csv("infectedrate weekly.csv")
head(data)
str(data)
data_val <- read.csv("infectedrate_val_weekly.csv")
head(data_val)
str(data_val)
n_stations = length(coordinates$ID)
n_stations_val = length(coordinates_val$ID)
n_data = length(data$ID)
n_data_val = length(data_val$ID )
n_days = as.integer(n_data/n_stations)
n_days_val = as.integer(n_data_val/n_stations_val )
mean_covariates = apply(data[,5:17],2,mean )
sd_covariates = apply(data[,5:17],2,sd)
data[,5:17] = scale(data[,5:17], mean_covariates,sd_covariates)
mean_covariates_val = apply (data_val[,5:17],2,mean)
sd_covariates_val = apply(data_val[,5:17],2,sd)
data_val[,5:17] = scale(data_val[,5:17],mean_covariates_val,sd_covariates_val)
data$loginfected = log(data$Infected.rate)
data_val$loginfected = log(data_val$infectedrate_val)
data$time = rep(1:n_days, each = n_stations)
data_val$time = rep(1:n_days_val, each = n_stations_val)
loc1=SpatialPoints(as.matrix(cbind(coordinates$X,coordinates$Y)))
loc2=SpatialPoints(BB)
borders2=rbind(BB,coordinates[,3:4])
loc3=SpatialPoints(borders2)
mesh = fmesher::fm_mesh_2d_inla(loc = cbind ( coordinates $X , coordinates $Y )
                                ,loc.domain = loc3, offset =c(10, 140),max.edge =c(50,1000) ,min.angle=c(27,21))

I would greatly appreciate your assistance in resolving this matter.

Thank you in advance.
Regards,
Flavian

The only relevant mention in that book chapter seems to be the sum-to-zero constraint, but that's applied automatically by inla; use constr=TRUE in the rw2 model to be explicit about it.

(You can also implement precisely what you ask for, with model generic0, and the design mTrix as an "A" matrix in a inla.stack construction, just like for the spde models (see examples online), but easier in the inlabru interface, where the design  matrix can used as the component input, and specifying mapper=bru_mapper_matrix() )

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Mesh creation using use “fmesher::fm_mesh_2d_inla()”function
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Mesh creation using use “fmesher::fm_mesh_2d_inla()”function
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
first of all, check your coordinate units and make sure the offset and
max.edge values are reasonable. I'm guessing your coordinates are in
metres? Then it depends on the size of your domain what values are
reasonable, but I suspect that offset 10 is much too small; Normally,
the offset would be _larger_ than max.edge, not smaller.
Also, please try with min.angle=21, to make sure that's not the issue;
21 is the largest value for which the algorithm is guaranteed to
terminate.

Also set the max.n.strict and max.n arguments to limit the allowed
total number of mesh vertices (set e.g. to 10000). This should cause
it to stop after adding too many points. That way, if it _still_ takes
a long time to run, we'll know there's some other problem.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

reading the random walks documentation (inla.doc("rw1")) I noticed the "values" argument, which is also described in Gomez-Rubio's INLA book ( Chapter 3 Mixed-effects Models | Bayesian inference with INLA (becarioprecario.bitbucket.io) <https://becarioprecario.bitbucket.io/inla-gitbook/ch-mixed.html#random-walks-rw1-and-rw2-models>). However, only a few words are utilized in both the documentation to describe the role of this argument. Could you give more information about it? or any suggestions for where to look more thoroughly (further examples, explanations,...).

I am particularly interested in applying it with an "iid" model as Muff. et al. did in the attached paper (Supplementary Material for “Bayesian analysis of measurement error models using INLA”).

Kind regards,
Chiara

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your reply, Finn. I'll try to give precisions "inline" below in italics.

> it's not entirely clear from the code what kind of observation model
> you're intending to use, but presumably you are using the actual
> _locations_ of points within each plot, so it's a point process model
> over the "space-times-size" product domain?

--> Indeed, the data collection was done in a 'point count distance sampling' setting, and
we are using the actual locations of observations within these 5-km radius plots.

> That's at least what the code is setup to do, and I don't see anything
> immediately wrong with the structure.
>
> A general observation: Setting a more specific prior distribution on
> log.r would likely help, as I expect it to be strongly confounded with
> the Intercept. See the development version of inlabru that has a new
> feature for converting components into non-Gaussians (via
> marginal=bru_mapper_marginal(...)).

--> I have to admit that I don't really understand where / how to pass that information about the prior distribution
on log.r . Could you please expand on that, or point me to the corresponding documentation ?

> With the CRAN version, at least do log.r(1, prec.linear = 1) or
> similar, to discourage extreme values.

--> That I understand ;-) . I will try this.

>
> The predict() step should be insensitive to the integration scheme,
> but the modelling step might be more sensitive.
> Might be sensible to plot the integration scheme to see what it's doing?
>
> Use
> ips <- fm_int(domain = list(size=size_domain,
> geometry=geometry_domain), samplers = plots22_sf)
> ggplot() + gg(geometry_domain) + geom_sf(data=ips %>% filter(size ==
> size_domain$loc[1]), aes(size = weight))
>
> The one part I'm uncertain about is your predict() fm_int construction, with
> samplers = list(
> size = NULL,
> geometry = plots22_sf # 101 survey points
> )
>
> Do you get the same integration points if you set
> samplers = list(
> geometry = plots22_sf # 101 survey points
> )

--> Yes, I get the same integration points with the two versions of the code above.

>
> Specifically, what happens with "size" in the fm_int() output?
> You do need size to be _something_ in the integration points; unclear
> if you want to predict for a specific size, or integrate over all of
> them.

--> What we really want to estimate / predict is the number of groups and
corresponding numbers of animals, over the whole study area.

--> Because of this, I take it that the integration points should "cover" the
whole study area ... Should I then use the sampling plots, or the boundary of the study area
to pass the `samplers ` argument in building the integration points?

--> From what I understand, in order to get the number of groups, I need to marginalize
over group size, ie to divide in the formula by the number of points along the size dimension.
In my case, that would be the "basis degree of freedom" from my object size_domain.
Is that correct ? But then, what should that "divider" be if I use the boundary of the sampling area
as samplers  ?

Thank you again for all your invaluable help!

Olivier

messages.body_plain:
You need to specify the component model as well:
Componentname(the matrix, model=“generic0”, Cmatrix=K1, mapper=…, hyper=…)
You should also specify the prior for the precision scaling parameter so you know exactly what it is.
“Comparisons” between frequentist spline estimations and bayesian Gaussian process model estimation only makes sense if you know exactly what you’re comparing, and why. There’s freq\bayes, but also spline/GP, and specific numerical implementation. Don’t do comparisons if you don’t understand the differences between those aspects.
Finn

The invalid factor level error indicates you need to use numerical indexing and not named indexing for the matrix columns. Just skip the argument to bru_mapper_matrix(), I think. I’ve never seen this specific error message before.

My comment about comparisons is because we see a _lot_ of ill-defined comparisons that are then used to give invalid advice about what model/methods are “better” than others. Since it’s not clear what you _are_ trying to compare, I can only give the general warning that comparisons are in general non-trivial.

Finn

According to the documentation, I have to pass the column labels for matrix mapping and it is not an optional parameter. I am using inlabru 2.9.0

> The invalid factor level error indicates you need to use numerical indexing and not named indexing for the matrix columns. Just skip the argument to bru_mapper_matrix(), I think. I’ve never seen this specific error message before.
>
> My comment about comparisons is because we see a _lot_ of ill-defined comparisons that are then used to give invalid advice about what model/methods are “better” than others. Since it’s not clear what you _are_ trying to compare, I can only give the general warning that comparisons are in general non-trivial.

> > > You need to specify the component model as well:
> > > Componentname(the matrix, model=“generic0”, Cmatrix=K1, mapper=…, hyper=…)
> > > You should also specify the prior for the precision scaling parameter so you know exactly what it is.
> > > “Comparisons” between frequentist spline estimations and bayesian Gaussian process model estimation only makes sense if you know exactly what you’re comparing, and why. messages.body_plain:
Ah, I see. That’s an oversight due to the original use case for that mapper (to be used with model=“fixed” for general linear model formulas).
You can instead define the component with just
Componentname(seq_len(nrow(K1)), model=“generic0”, Cmatrix=K1)
and in the predictor expression use
…+X1%*%Componentname+…
(The predictor expression is a general R expression.j

I’ll need to fix the matrix mapper to handle this use case.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chiara,

The 'values' argument is a little tricky

f(idx, model="..", values=c(...))

WITHOUT 'values', then 'values' looks at the unique sorted values of
'idx', and create the model on these 'locations'.

However, some models, have default values set, like 'besag'

> inla.models()$latent$besag$set.default.values
[1] TRUE

which takes the values from the size of the graph.

wheras other models do not, like 'rw2'

> inla.models()$latent$rw2$set.default.values
[1] FALSE

which take its values as  unique(sort(idx))

Sometimes the values of 'idx' is NOT representative for the model or
where you need to it be, so then we need to set 'values' to the
locations we need to model to be defined.

One such example, is where data is defined as

x <- c(4, 8, 16)
y = c(4, 0, 16)

where (x[i],y[i]) is a point, then we would like to construct and
interpolating spline, which obviously needs more points than 3.

the attached examples demonstrate how this is done.

Havard

K1 needs to be in the evaluation environment. Put it as a regular
variable in the calling workspace (technically, in the environment
where you create the component). R variable scoping is messy. Do
something that works.
There are probably cleaner ways, but I'd need a regexp::regexp()
report on github to track&improve specific behaviour when I have time.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Like Haavard asked, are you sure you actually need it, or are you
really looking for things like "the marginal variance at each location
of interest"?

The information needed to compute these quantities is available, but
in a way that's more amenable to the internal methods that know how to
make use of them; the conditional posterior precision matrix for the
joint latent field conditionally on each hyperparameter integration
point is available, for example (via $misc$config).

>From inlabru, what we tend to do is to call generate() or predict(),
that internally call inla.posterior.sample() that knows how to use the
information. By specifying an evaluation expression (like the formula
to bru()) you can get posterior samples from any linear or nonlinear
expression involving the model components, and predict() produces
summaries of that (like posterior means and standard deviations).

Finn

Il giorno venerdì 27 ottobre 2023 alle 17:54:37 UTC+2 Finn Lindgren ha scritto:
> Like Haavard asked, are you sure you actually need it, or are you
> really looking for things like "the marginal variance at each location
> of interest"?
>
> The information needed to compute these quantities is available, but
> in a way that's more amenable to the internal methods that know how to
> make use of them; the conditional posterior precision matrix for the
> joint latent field conditionally on each hyperparameter integration
> point is available, for example (via $misc$config).
>
> From inlabru, what we tend to do is to call generate() or predict(),
> that internally call inla.posterior.sample() that knows how to use the
> information. By specifying an evaluation expression (like the formula
> to bru()) you can get posterior samples from any linear or nonlinear
> expression involving the model components, and predict() produces
> summaries of that (like posterior means and standard deviations).
>
> Finn

messages.subject: Re: Time varying covariates in cox model
messages.subject_clean: Time varying covariates in cox model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Yes it's possible, the trick is to decompose the follow-up into intervals (as done with Cox) and and use left truncation / right censoring for the intervals in-between entry and event time. For example I have an event at time 3, I can create 3 intervals: 0->1 (right censored), 1->2 (left truncated and right censored) and 2->3 (left truncated and observed event). Then each interval can have a different value for the time-varying covariate.
Best,
Denis Rustand
he...@r-inla.org
